column4: This ayah gathers the section's whole bodily arc: dust, sperm, clot, a formed or unformed lump, settlement in wombs to a fixed term, childhood, maturity, death or decrepit age; its closing revival of dead earth also places body and pasture in one scene.

The waiting period of three قُرُوءٍ uses the ق ر ء family named by the section, while the same ayah forbids women to hide what Allah has created in their wombs; reproductive time, uterine enclosure, and divine creation meet directly.
Allah knows what every female bears, what wombs diminish or increase, and declares that everything with Him has a measure; this joins the hidden womb to the section's قدّر as exact apportioning.
The fetus is made خَلْقًا مِّنۢ بَعْدِ خَلْقٍۢ inside three darknesses, making the section's gathering, stage-by-stage formation, and enclosing womb visible.
The drop is placed فِى قَرَارٍۢ مَّكِينٍۢ, a secure lodging that concretizes the womb closing around and holding the developing child; 23:14 supplies the transformations within it.
The drop becomes clot, lump, bones, and clothed flesh before being produced as another creation; it expands the section's خلق and سوى into a bodily sequence, continuing 23:13's secure womb.
The exact pair فَخَلَقَ فَسَوَّىٰ is applied to the clot, explicitly confirming the section's hearing of 87:2 as fetal creation and bodily ordering.
The question أَلَمْ نَخْلُقكُّم مِّن مَّآءٍۢ مَّهِينٍۢ begins a compact gestational sequence; 77:21-23 identify the secure womb, term, and measure.
Allah places the reproductive fluid فِى قَرَارٍۢ مَّكِينٍۢ, the same secure-womb image that makes the section's sense of uterine gathering concrete; 77:22 gives its limit.
The embryo remains until قَدَرٍۢ مَّعْلُومٍۢ, a known measure or term, joining enclosure to the section's claim that each bodily phase is apportioned.
فَقَدَرْنَا follows the fluid, secure lodging, and known term, so the ق د ر root is bodily measure and divine power at once, precisely the semantic meeting developed in the section.
مِن نُّطْفَةٍ خَلَقَهُۥ فَقَدَّرَهُۥ applies creation and exact determination to the sperm-drop, directly aligning bodily origin with the section's خلق and قدّر.
After 80:19's خلق and قدّر, ثُمَّ ٱلسَّبِيلَ يَسَّرَهُۥ adds an eased way; it echoes the section's sequence of measure, guidance, and ease and may also suggest the way out at birth.

Dust, sperm, clot, emergence as a child, full strength, old age, death, and an appointed term are set in one ayah, matching the section's reading of the surah's word families as an entire human lifespan.

Human life is explicitly ordered as weakness, strength, then weakness and grey hair; the second weakness reverses bodily completion and gives the section's maturation-to-old-age arc its clearest formulation.

Creation from dust and then a drop is joined to pairing, every conception and birth under Allah's knowledge, and every extended or shortened life recorded; formation and measured lifespan are one act.
هُوَ ٱلَّذِى يُصَوِّرُكُمْ فِى ٱلْأَرْحَامِ كَيْفَ يَشَآءُ locates divinely willed bodily form inside the womb, clarifying what the section means by the fetus acquiring its shape.
Allah knows humans when He brings them from earth and when they are أَجِنَّةٌۭ فِى بُطُونِ أُمَّهَٰتِكُمْ; the named fetus in the mother's body makes the section's hidden bodily stage explicit.
A light pregnancy becomes heavy before the parents ask for a sound child, presenting gestation as gradual bodily accumulation and completion within the single-soul creation story.
Painful carrying and delivery, thirty months of carrying and weaning, full strength, and the age of forty turn the section's bodily word-family sequence into a continuous lived chronology.
ثُمَّ سَوَّىٰهُۥ joins bodily proportioning to the breath of spirit and the gift of hearing, sight, and hearts; the ordered body becomes a living, perceiving human.
Human progeny is made from an extract of lowly fluid; it supplies the reproductive material that 32:9 then proportions and animates.
Allah perfects everything He creates and begins human creation from clay; 32:8-9 narrow that general perfection into reproductive fluid and the proportioned body.
The human was a sperm-drop from emitted semen, the concrete first stage that becomes clot and is created and proportioned in 75:38.
The created, proportioned embryo becomes the male and female pair, completing the bodily differentiation begun in 75:37-38 before the resurrection question of 75:40.
The maker of the embryo is asked whether He is بِقَٰدِرٍ to revive the dead; bodily measure opens into power, and first creation becomes evidence for re-creation.
ٱلَّذِى خَلَقَكَ فَسَوَّىٰكَ فَعَدَلَكَ directly addresses the human as created, proportioned, and balanced, giving the section's bodily sense of سوى an exact parallel.
فِىٓ أَىِّ صُورَةٍۢ مَّا شَآءَ رَكَّبَكَ adds chosen form and bodily composition to 82:7's creation and balance, specifying the result of divine ordering.
The garden owner's companion recalls creation from dust, then a drop, then ثُمَّ سَوَّىٰكَ رَجُلًا; bodily formation is the argument against self-secure confidence in the garden.
وَقَدْ خَلَقَكُمْ أَطْوَارًا states that humans were created in successive stages, succinctly naming the section's womb-to-age reading.
The human is created from a mixed drop and made hearing and seeing for a test; bodily formation is presented as fitted capacity and purpose rather than mere growth.
Allah brings humans from their mothers' wombs knowing nothing and gives hearing, sight, and hearts, marking the passage from enclosed fetus to equipped living person.
بَلَغَ أَشُدَّهُۥ وَٱسْتَوَىٰ uses the سوى family at the arrival of full strength and maturity, exactly matching the section's secondary dictionary sense of completed youth.
إِمَّا يَبْلُغَنَّ عِندَكَ ٱلْكِبَرَ places one or both parents in old age under the grown child's care, making the ك ب ر family's bodily life-stage sense ethically concrete.
The prayer كَمَا رَبَّيَانِى صَغِيرًا uses the ر ب ب family for parents raising a small child; beside 17:23's aged parents, nurture and decline become the two ends of one life cycle.
Old age reaches the owner of a fruitful garden while his children are weak, and fire destroys the garden; aged body, dependent offspring, vegetation, and perishing provision meet in one warning.

Mary's Lord accepts her and أَنۢبَتَهَا نَبَاتًا حَسَنًا, causing her to grow as a good growth under care; divine nurture of a child is expressed through the plant image that the section pairs with bodily growth.

Pharaoh asks Moses أَلَمْ نُرَبِّكَ فِينَا وَلِيدًا, using the ر ب ب family for a human ruler's claim to have raised an infant; it clarifies the nurture sense while contrasting human patronage with the true Lord.
وَٱللَّهُ أَنۢبَتَكُم مِّنَ ٱلْأَرْضِ نَبَاتًا describes human creation itself as plant growth from earth, making the section's body–pasture analogy explicit rather than merely adjacent.
Humans are returned into earth and brought forth again, so 71:17's bodily plant-growth image continues through death and resurrection.
Creation فِىٓ أَحْسَنِ تَقْوِيمٍ gives a compact statement of the well-set, sound human form developed under the section's سوى sense.

ثُمَّ رَدَدْنَٰهُ أَسْفَلَ سَٰفِلِينَ reverses 95:4's best constitution; whether read as bodily decrepitude or a final abasement, it marks the limit of perfected form rather than allowing it to seem permanent.
Worldly life is water-grown vegetation that mingles, then becomes dry fragments scattered by wind; it is the exact withering-garden counterpart to the ordered body in 18:37.
The stages of worldly life culminate in the rain-plant image: growth pleases, yellows, and becomes debris; human social maturation and vegetation's decline are compressed into the same warning.
The likeness of worldly life joins rain, earth's growth, human and animal food, full adornment, and sudden cutting down; it illuminates the section's move from formed body to transient pasture.
Rain is conducted through earth, crops vary in color, then yellow and crumble; the visible sequence supplies a vegetal analogue for the body's measured growth and decline.
From earth humans are created, into it returned, and from it brought out again, joining bodily origin, death, and renewed emergence in the same ground on which vegetation grows.
Human creation begins from an extract of clay, supplying the earthly starting material for 23:13-14's womb and bodily transformations.
After the ordered prenatal sequence, the human must die; this gives bodily completion its temporal boundary.
After death comes resurrection, completing the creation–death–re-creation arc begun in 23:12-14.
Allah creates and causes death, and some are returned to the most abject age until knowledge is lost; bodily and mental decline follow the section's stage of maturity.
Whomever Allah grants long life He reverses فِى ٱلْخَلْقِ, so ageing is presented as an undoing within creation itself, a direct counter-motion to bodily completion.
The mother carries the child in weakness upon weakness and weans in two years, adding maternal bodily cost and early nurture to the section's prenatal-to-childhood sequence.
Allah grants daughters or sons as He wills; the completed body's sex and the gift of offspring remain under the Creator's apportioning.
Allah may pair sons and daughters or make someone barren, stating the reproductive boundary around 42:49's gifts and showing that bodily creation is willed, not automatic.
Allah creates the male and female pair, specifying sexual differentiation as part of bodily creation.
The pair comes مِن نُّطْفَةٍ إِذَا تُمْنَىٰ, locating that differentiation in the emitted reproductive drop.
The human is commanded to consider from what he was created, opening a bodily-origin argument that 86:6-8 carries from fluid to return.
Creation is from gushing fluid, another direct presentation of the reproductive material gathered and formed in the womb.
The fluid's emergence from between the backbone and ribs keeps attention on the embodied source of generation; 86:8 turns that origin into evidence of return.
إِنَّهُۥ عَلَىٰ رَجْعِهِۦ لَقَادِرٌ makes divine power to return the human the conclusion of the reproductive-fluid scene, paralleling 75:37-40.
Human creation from a sperm-drop is immediately set against the resulting person's open disputation; the fully articulate adversary is traced back to a minute bodily beginning.
The human created from a sperm-drop becomes an open opponent, setting developed agency against its fragile origin before the bone-and-resurrection dispute.
The disputant forgets his own creation and asks who can revive decayed bones; the section's formed body becomes the forgotten premise of his objection.
The answer is that the One who produced the bones the first time will revive them, explicitly making initial bodily formation the measure of re-creation.
أَفَرَءَيْتُم مَّا تُمْنُونَ asks the addressees to inspect the reproductive fluid they emit, grounding the creation argument in their own bodily act.
The question contrasts human emission with divine creation: أَءَنتُمْ تَخْلُقُونَهُۥٓ أَمْ نَحْنُ ٱلْخَٰلِقُونَ; it separates material contribution from the forming act.
Death is apportioned among humans, extending measured creation into a measured end and leading toward transformed re-creation.
Allah can replace people's likenesses and produce them in a form they do not know, placing bodily form within divine power rather than fixed human possession.
Knowledge of the first creation is invoked as the reason to remember, completing the sequence from emitted fluid through death to another production.

ٱقْرَأْ uses the ق ر ء root and names the Lord who creates; 96:2 immediately puts that act of reading beside human embryonic origin, an especially close meeting with the section's secondary uterine sense.
خَلَقَ ٱلْإِنسَٰنَ مِنْ عَلَقٍ gives the clot as human origin beside 96:1's ق ر ء imperative, bringing the root's reading sense and the section's womb sense into one two-ayah opening.
رَبُّنَا ٱلَّذِىٓ أَعْطَىٰ كُلَّ شَىْءٍ خَلْقَهُۥ ثُمَّ هَدَىٰ joins Lord, each thing's fitted creation, and guidance, closely restating the logic of 87:1-3 that the section applies to the body.
Allah creates everything and فَقَدَّرَهُۥ تَقْدِيرًا, an exact formulation of the section's definition of placing each thing in its particular measure and form.
إِنَّا كُلَّ شَىْءٍ خَلَقْنَٰهُ بِقَدَرٍ states creation by measure universally, giving the bodily measurements in the section their wider principle.

قَدْ جَعَلَ ٱللَّهُ لِكُلِّ شَىْءٍۢ قَدْرًا states that Allah has assigned a measure to everything; in its provision-and-trust context it broadens, without bodily detail, the exact apportioning used for gestation.
No female conceives or gives birth except with Allah's knowledge; conception and emergence are framed as known events within the measured bodily process.
Knowledge of what is in the wombs belongs to Allah, emphasizing the hiddenness of the very formation that the section unfolds through word families.
Allah forms humans and makes their forms good, joining deliberate bodily configuration to a judgment of fitness and beauty.
وَصَوَّرَكُمْ فَأَحْسَنَ صُوَرَكُمْ links good bodily form, provision, and Allah as Lord, reinforcing the section's sound-body and nurturing-Rabb senses together.
Allah says He created and then shaped humankind before the command concerning Adam, presenting bodily form as a distinct completion within creation.
The command follows فَإِذَا سَوَّيْتُهُۥ وَنَفَخْتُ فِيهِ مِن رُّوحِى; bodily proportioning precedes animation, clarifying سوى as preparation of a formed human body.
The repeated formula of proportioning the clay human and breathing spirit makes the completed form the threshold between fashioned body and living person.
The oath by the soul and the One who سَوَّىٰهَا extends the section's proportioning verb from body to self or soul; the changed object suggests that human ordering is inward as well as anatomical.
The statement that the human was created weak supplies the vulnerable bodily condition from which the section's growth toward soundness and strength proceeds.
The question whether Allah made two eyes gives a concrete anatomical instance of the fitted body implied by سوى.
A tongue and two lips continue 90:8's inventory of paired and coordinated organs, showing bodily ordering as equipment for human action.
أَيَحْسَبُ ٱلْإِنسَٰنُ أَن يُتْرَكَ سُدًى denies that the human will be left aimless; 75:37-40 make his measured embryonic creation the proof of accountability and return.
The question whether humans thought they were created aimlessly and would not be returned states explicitly the purpose-and-resurrection claim implicit in the section's ordered body.
After 40:67's complete sequence of bodily ages, هُوَ ٱلَّذِى يُحْىِۦ وَيُمِيتُ names the giver of life and death and grounds every stage in His decree.
Creation from clay is followed by a decreed term and another term known to Allah, linking bodily origin to measured duration even though prenatal stages are not shown.
The summons to reflect within themselves leads to creation in truth and for a named term; it turns embodied self-knowledge into recognition that created life has a limit and purpose.
Zechariah asks how he can have a boy when بَلَغَنِىَ ٱلْكِبَرُ and his wife is barren; old age and new gestation meet as a divinely crossed bodily boundary.
Sarah's amazement joins her own old age to an aged husband at the announcement of a child, placing birth at the far end of the ordinary life sequence.
Abraham praises Allah for granting Ishmael and Isaac عَلَى ٱلْكِبَرِ; offspring arriving in old age makes the section's two distant bodily stages coincide.
Abraham asks whether he is being given good news عَلَىٰٓ أَن مَّسَّنِىَ ٱلْكِبَرُ, explicitly making old age the apparent boundary challenged by the promised birth.
Zechariah describes weakened bones and a head aflame with grey hair while asking for an heir; bodily signs of decline precede the promised child's beginning.
His wife is barren and he has reached مِنَ ٱلْكِبَرِ عِتِيًّا, so the possibility of a child is placed beyond ordinary reproductive ageing.
The answer recalls that the Lord created Zechariah before when he was nothing; first creation answers the old man's doubt about a new birth, just as it answers doubt about resurrection.
The woman calls herself عَجُوزٌ عَقِيمٌ, an old barren woman, marking the ordinary bodily limit against which the birth announcement stands.
Mary asks how she can have a child when no man has touched her, and the answer is that Allah creates what He wills; the ayah marks divine creation beyond the ordinary sperm-to-womb route.
Jesus is likened to Adam, whom Allah created from dust and commanded to be; this gives the section's gestational sequence a clear exception without weakening divine authorship of form.
Mary names the absence of male contact and unchastity, defining the ordinary reproductive condition that this conception will cross.
The promised boy is made a sign and mercy and the matter is decreed; bodily creation without the ordinary father is presented as an intentional boundary case, not an accident.
Mary conceives and withdraws to a distant place, restoring a real pregnancy and enclosed bodily development after the exceptional conception.
Labor pains drive Mary to the palm trunk, giving the approach and crisis of birth the concrete bodily scene suggested by the section's secondary sense of nearness to delivery.
The chaste woman receives the breathed spirit and she and her son become a sign; womb-bearing is retained while ordinary generation is exceeded.
Mary's guarded chastity and the breathed spirit again locate exceptional creation in her body, clarifying that divine formation is not confined to the usual reproductive means.
Bones are raised and clothed with flesh before the observer sees that Allah is powerful over all things; bodily reassembly mirrors prenatal building while proving resurrection.
The objection asks whether, once lost in earth, humans can be in a new creation; beside 32:7-9's first bodily formation, it exposes the disbelief that the earlier sequence answers.
The question about becoming bones and fragments and then being raised as a new creation makes bodily decomposition the apparent obstacle.
The answer to 17:49 is that the One who originated them the first time will return them, using first bodily creation as the decisive comparison.
The human asks whether, after dying, he will be brought out alive; the doubt focuses directly on continuity of the body across death.
The answer recalls that Allah created the person before when he was nothing, making initial creation the precedent for renewed life.
The addressees are asked to see how Allah begins creation and then repeats it, stating the same first-formation argument that the section draws from the fetus.
Travel through the earth is commanded to inspect how creation began, after which Allah produces the final creation; bodily return is placed within observable created origins.
The question whether Allah tired in the first creation exposes confusion about a new creation; initial forming power is the measure of re-creation.
كَمَا بَدَأْنَآ أَوَّلَ خَلْقٍۢ نُّعِيدُهُۥ promises to repeat creation as it began, turning the section's first bodily formation into a pattern for the end.
Allah begins creation and repeats it before the return of all, a concise statement of the relation made bodily and evidential in 75:37-40.
The question asks who begins creation and then repeats it; in its provision context, renewed creation belongs to the same ordering power that sustains embodied life.
Allah begins creation, repeats it, and then humans are returned to Him, extending the body's measured beginning to its final destination.
Originating and repeating creation are attributed to Allah, and repetition is described as easier; the ayah generalizes the fetus-to-resurrection inference.
إِنَّهُۥ هُوَ يُبْدِئُ وَيُعِيدُ gives the beginning and return of creation as one divine action, a compressed counterpart to the section's life arc.
بَلْ تُحِبُّونَ ٱلْعَاجِلَةَ names love of the immediate life; within the same surah, 75:37-40 grounds the rebuke in fetal origin and resurrection power.
وَتَذَرُونَ ٱلْـَٔاخِرَةَ gives the abandoned lasting horizon against 75:20's immediate life, completing the same preference contrast as 87:16-17 before the surah turns to bodily creation.
The garden owner doubts the Hour and assumes a favorable return; 18:37 answers with his dust-and-drop origin, so denial of return is exposed by the ordered body he inhabits.
The garden's produce is encompassed and its owner wrings his hands over the ruined trellises; it realizes the destruction that stands between 18:37's formed man and 18:45's withered-world image.
A period passed when the human was not a thing mentioned; 76:2 then supplies the mixed drop, so bodily stages begin from nonexistence rather than from an already formed self.
Creation from a single soul, its mate, and the dispersal of many men and women frames individual gestation within the multiplication of one human family and explicitly invokes womb-ties.

Humanity is produced from a single soul and given a place of settlement and deposit; these have been read in bodily and womb-related ways, but the ayah itself leaves the locations unstated, so the uterine connection remains uncertain.
Humans are produced from earth and caused to dwell and flourish in it; the earthly origin and cultivation verb support the section's meeting of formed body and growing ground.
Allah is the One who brought humans into being and made hearing, sight, and hearts for them, another concrete account of the ordered body as equipped life.
Hearing, sight, and hearts are attributed to the One who produced humankind; within the surah that narrated fetal formation in 23:12-14, these faculties show what that formed body becomes.
